g.text: Benchmarking wkv & wbftree against mainstream embedded databases
Key/Value Spec：24B Key / 150B Value, binary keys and serialized payloads.
Cache Budget：Uniformly configured to 128 MiB, constraining read cache, buffer
pool, and write buffer across engines.
Workload Scale：6,000,000 records (~1.04 GiB raw writes), data size 10~30x
Write Scenarios：Durable per-transaction writes by default (commit triggers
fsync, matching the upstream redb-bench default sync=true); benchmarks evaluate
individual, batch (1,000 items/batch), plus a nosync section with per-commit
fsync disabled for async throughput comparison, restoring durable writes
Read Benchmarks：100,000 point lookups and 5,000 range scans (step 10), multi-threaded
reads (4~32 threads), reporting median of 3 runs.
Disk & Memory：Disk usage measures physical file size pre/post compaction;
memory records resident physical memory (RSS / Footprint).
Performance metrics display relative multiplier in the first line (baseline
1.00X for lowest performance, higher is better) and disk throughput in the
second line. Random reads and range scans report median of 3 runs. Cache
sizes are configured uniformly where applicable. All write sections except
nosync perform durable per-transaction fsync; the nosync section disables
per-commit fsync via set_sync(false) and restores durable writes afterwards.
The total-records (len) row mixes counting semantics — rocksdb/sqlite/fjall
count via full-table or LSM iterator scans, wkv counts via an in-memory
hash-index bucket-chain scan, while redb/wbftree read a metadata counter
directly; multipliers on this row reflect counting-semantics differences,
not engine performance, and must not be read as a performance conclusion.
All write sections (bulk load, individual writes, batch writes, nosync,
removals) are timed once each with no warmup discard window and no repeated
sampling, so the figures include first-touch page-fault and cold-cache effects
and are not reproducible means. The wbftree uncompacted-size row uses a
page-level write-through caliber with no explicit flush step (upstream bf-tree
exposes no page-pool drain API); its size is permanently underreported by
a sub-0.2% buffer-tail residue relative to a fully solidified snapshot image,
a constant that does not scale with dataset size — interpret cross-engine
